THOUGHT: The patient is a 31-year-old woman with chronic intermittent flank pain, recurrent UTIs (5 in 2 years), and now newly identified hypertension (150/88 mmHg) and renal insufficiency (elevated BUN 29 mg/dL and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL). Physical exam reveals nontender, bilaterally enlarged upper abdominal masses — consistent with enlarged kidneys — and renal ultrasound shows “bilaterally enlarged kidneys with multiple parenchymal anechoic masses.” Anechoic masses on renal ultrasound are highly suggestive of cysts. In a young adult with bilateral renal enlargement, multiple cysts, hypertension, flank pain, and progressive renal dysfunction (elevated creatinine), the most likely diagnosis is autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Although ADPKD typically presents in the 3rd–4th decade, onset in the early 30s is common, and extrarenal manifestations (e.g., liver cysts, intracranial aneurysms) may be absent or unrecognized early on. Recurrent UTIs can occur due to cyst infection or urinary stasis from distorted anatomy. Hypertension is often an early manifestation of ADPKD, driven by intrarenal renin-angiotensin activation. The absence of prior stone history, family history (though patient reports “no known familial kidney disease” — which may reflect incomplete knowledge or de novo mutation), and normal prior health does not exclude ADPKD; ~25% of cases arise from *de novo* PKD1 mutations. Other considerations — such as acquired cystic kidney disease (unlikely without ESRD/long-term dialysis), medullary sponge kidney (typically unilateral, no renal enlargement, associated with stones), or multicystic dysplastic kidney (usually unilateral and diagnosed in childhood) — are inconsistent with this presentation. Simple cysts are usually solitary or few, not bilateral and numerous with renal enlargement and functional impairment.

DIAGNOSIS: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
